title: The vagus and the gut's own brain
objective: Place the vagus nerve and the enteric nervous system in the gut-sensing picture.

steps.title: Three players in the gut wall
steps.body:
Gut function involves three distinct neural systems:

- the **[[vagus nerve]]** (parasympathetic motor + vagal sensory afferents),
- **spinal [[DRG]]** afferents entering the cord,
- the **[[enteric nervous system]]** — the gut's own network of neurons in the bowel wall, which can run local reflexes on its own.

Extrinsic afferents (vagal, spinal) talk to this intrinsic system.

steps.prompt: Which system can coordinate basic gut motility even without input from the brain?
steps.explanation: The enteric nervous system is often called the gut's 'second brain' because its local circuits can drive motility reflexes autonomously — then extrinsic nerves modulate and report on it.

steps.setup: Recent work describes an enteric-to-DRG pathway: enteric neurons relaying signals to spinal (DRG) afferents (see Field Pulse).
options: It shows the DRG is part of the CNS
It means DRG afferents may not only sense the gut wall directly, but also receive relayed input from the enteric system
It proves the vagus is unnecessary
It has nothing to do with sensing
steps.reveal: It adds a layer: the gut's own neurons can feed the spinal (DRG) sensory line, not just the wall mechanics. A fresh wrinkle in exactly your lab's circuit — and why the three systems here are worth keeping distinct.

reviewNotes: Connects D-track anatomy to the Field Pulse enteric-DRG paper and B8.
